{{Short description|Game theory concept}}
In [[game theory]] and related fields, a '''game form''', '''game frame''', '''ruleset''', or '''outcome function''' is the set of [[Game rule|rules]] that govern a game and determine its outcome based on each player's choices. A game form differs from a game in that it does not stipulate the [[utility|utilities]] or payoffs for each agent.<ref name=":1" />

[[Mathematics|Mathematically]], a game form can be defined as a [[Map (mathematics)|mapping]] going [[Domain of a function|from]] an ''action'' ''space<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Roth |first1=Benjamin N. |last2=Shorrer |first2=Ran I. |date=March 2015 |title=Mechanism Design in the Presence of a Pre-Existing Game |url=https://ideas.repec.org//p/qsh/wpaper/240431.html |journal=Working Paper |language=en}}</ref>''<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Blumrosen |first1=Liad |last2=Feldman |first2=Michal |date=2013-11-01 |title=Mechanism design with a restricted action space |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0899825613000481 |journal=Games and Economic Behavior |volume=82 |pages=424–443 |doi=10.1016/j.geb.2013.03.005 |issn=0899-8256|url-access=subscription }}</ref>—which describes all the possible moves a player can make—[[Codomain|to]] an ''outcome space''. The action space is also often called a ''message space'' when the actions consist of providing information about beliefs or preferences, in which case it is called a '''direct mechanism'''.<ref name=":0" /> For example, an [[electoral system]] is a game form mapping a message space consisting of [[ballot]]s to a winning candidate (the outcome).<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Gibbard |first=Allan |date=1978 |title=Straightforwardness of Game Forms with Lotteries as Outcomes |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1914235 |journal=Econometrica |volume=46 |issue=3 |pages=595–614 |doi=10.2307/1914235 |jstor=1914235 |issn=0012-9682|hdl=10419/220562 |hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Similarly, an [[auction]] is a game form that takes each [[Bid price|bidder's price]] and maps them to both a winner and a set of payments by the bidders.

Often, a game form is a set of rules or [[institution]]s designed to implement some [[Normative economics|normative]] goal (called a [[social choice function]]), by motivating [[Agent (economics)|agents]] to act in a particular way through an appropriate choice of [[incentive]]s. Then, the game form is called an '''implementation''' or '''[[Mechanism design|mechanism]]'''. This approach is widely used in the study of [[auction theory|auctions]] and [[electoral system]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ozdaglar |first=Asu |title=Game Theory with Engineering Applications |url=https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-254-game-theory-with-engineering-applications-spring-2010/12d5d265886971f472cdcead234687dd_MIT6_254S10_lec01.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240629182801/https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-254-game-theory-with-engineering-applications-Spring-2010/12d5d265886971f472cdcead234687dd_MIT6_254S10_lec01.pdf |archive-date=2024-06-29}}</ref>

The social choice function represents the desired outcome or goal of the game, such as maximizing social welfare or achieving a fair allocation of resources. The [[mechanism design]]er's task is to design the game form in such a way that when each player plays their best response (i.e. behaves strategically), the resulting equilibrium implements the desired social choice function.
